When you run through the official `anthropics/claude-code-action`, triggered by `@claude` on an
issue, pull request or review in this repository:

- The only commands you may run are the read-only `gh pr diff` and `gh pr view`, to read a pull

- Change request: work on a `claude/...` branch or on the pull request you were given, as the

## 4. Mandatory Operational Protocol: Entire + GitHub Enterprise Integration & Anti-Hang PR Flow (`LCV-517` / Ruleset ID `20582436`)

GitHub Enterprise and Entire run in parallel. Entire's architecture ([Entire docs](https://docs.entire.com/)) and the `LCV-517` sequence below are mandatory for full session and checkpoint capture and to keep Pull Requests from hanging on the Enterprise Rulesets ([rulesets](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets); `20582436` on `main`, `20613778` on every other branch).

### A. Entire Architecture, Hook Locations, Session Spawning, Crosslinking & Handoff

Entire captures agent sessions through repository-level agent hooks and links them to commits with the `Entire-Checkpoint` and `Entire-Attribution` trailers, stored under `refs/entire/checkpoints/*` or `entire/checkpoints/v1`.

1. **Hook configuration per agent, present before the session starts** (installed with `entire agent add <agent>` by the operator or on the operator's order, as the Cursor hooks were; agents never change hook configuration on their own): Antigravity CLI `.agents/hooks.json` plus the global title-feed wrapper in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json` (`entire hooks antigravity title-tee`); Claude Code `.claude/settings.json`; Codex `.codex/hooks.json`; Copilot CLI `.github/hooks/entire.json`; Cursor `.cursor/hooks.json` (operator decision, [Cursor hooks](https://cursor.com/docs/hooks)); external agents `"external_agents": true` in `.entire/settings.local.json`, honored only while that file is untracked (`entire agent-help session attach`). Running agent processes do not load hooks added after they started, and hooks capture only sessions that run inside the Git repository or worktree root where Entire is enabled.

2. **The `lcv-workspace` parent-folder problem.** The operator opens the IDEs at `C:\Users\lcvle\lcv-workspace\`, outside any repository root, where Entire's hooks capture nothing.

   > **BLOCKING GATE — Repository-Rooted Sub-Session (operator decision):** before editing any file, staging, or committing in a repository, the agent runs in a session whose working root is that repository's root or that worktree's root. A session started anywhere else opens a sub-session inside that root (commands below) and does the repository work there. The only alternative is Entire's native linking (`entire session adopt` from another worktree, or `entire session attach`, below), only when opening the sub-session is technically impossible, with the raw error recorded as proof. If neither is possible, stop: do not edit, commit, push, or open a Pull Request, and report the proof. Work done in violation of this gate is not delivered work. A sub-session runs the checkout's tracked hooks and configuration at startup, so never open one in a checkout of a branch not created by the operator or the agent (Section 3); review such a branch read-only from the agent's own checkout.

   Binding procedure:
   * Change the working directory to the exact repository root (`C:\Users\lcvle\lcv-workspace\<repo>`) or worktree (`C:\Users\lcvle\lcv-workspace\.worktrees\<worktree>`), strip inherited `GIT_DIR`, `GIT_WORK_TREE`, and `GIT_COMMON_DIR` ([git environment](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Internals-Environment-Variables)), and verify with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` ([git rev-parse](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-rev-parse)).

If the agent's hooks are missing or stale, run `entire doctor` for the diagnosis (its offer to fix is declined in the promptless terminal) and ask the operator to run `entire agent add <agent> --force`. In a fresh worktree, confirm that the directory named by `git config core.hooksPath` exists (for example `.husky/_`, Git-ignored and created by the repository's install step); without it no hook fires ([githooks](https://git-scm.com/docs/githooks)).

1. **SSH commit signing:** every commit created locally (`commit`, `amend`, `merge`) is signed with SSH (`git commit -S`, `gpg.format=ssh`, 1Password SSH signer, [1Password Git commit signing](https://www.1password.dev/ssh/git-commit-signing)); never GPG/OpenPGP for your own commits, and never create commits or pull requests through the API from a local session (commits with `git`, pull requests with `gh pr create`, Section 4.C). Whenever implementing changes and taking a Pull Request to merge, execute these five steps in this order:

* **Step 1: Branch & Development (inside the repository or worktree root)**

A worktree when the root has uncommitted work, is in use by another session, must stay on `main` for a live process (the `op run` terminal client in `github-operations`), or when several changes proceed in parallel; a new worktree contains only tracked files, so confirm its hooks and install artifacts first ([git worktree](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree)).

  2. `gh pr view <pr> --json mergeStateStatus` ([gh pr view](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_view)).

## 6. Zero-Tolerance Anti-Slop Engineering Protocol, Contract Surface Sweeps & 5-Stage Gatekeeper

"Slop" is avoidable, low-trust work caused by not understanding the repository well enough: unverified assumptions, lazy truncation, hallucinated interfaces, duplicate systems, type evasion and catch-all masking, premature abstraction, unrequested mutation, iteration debris, filler. Any violation below is a critical execution failure.

### A. Anti-Truncation & Complete Implementation
No placeholders, truncation markers, or elisions (`// TODO`, `// FIXME`, `// implement logic here`, `// ... rest of the code`, `/* existing code */`, `pass`). Every code block, script, or patch is complete, syntactically valid, fully imported, and immediately runnable. Never delegate mechanical work to the operator ("repeat this pattern", "add the imports").

### B. Epistemic Anti-Slop
Read the exact live state of a file, function, schema, or workflow and its nearby helpers and tests before writing or referencing it; reuse the repository's established pattern instead of a parallel helper or ad-hoc parser. Never guess library methods, CLI flags, GraphQL fields, environment variables, or SDK signatures: verify against the installed lockfile versions and the official documentation. Never hand-edit or regex a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `Cargo.lock`); regenerate only with the official tool, in the modes of Section 3.

### C. Architectural, Sequencing & Code Anti-Slop
Strict typing (`strict: true` in TypeScript, strict Python 3.10+ annotations, explicit Go/Rust types); never `any`, `as unknown as T`, `@ts-ignore`, `@ts-expect-error`, `# type: ignore`, or loose `Record<string, any>`: fix the contract. No empty `catch {}`, no log-and-continue that corrupts state, no silent fallbacks (`|| "default"`, `?? 0`) for missing business configuration, credentials, or market prices: fail fast with structured, secret-free logging. No inconsistent, orphaned, or lost state when a later step fails; no irreversible write before a fallible call; cleanup on success and failure; tests use isolated directories or repositories inside `temp/` and never touch the operator's real config, keychain, or checkout. No speculative abstractions, single-implementation interfaces, wrapper classes, or heavy patterns for linear problems: flat, readable, immutable, pure, modular code (SRP, DRY). No accidental $O(N^2)$ loops, N+1 queries, unindexed lookups, unbounded accumulations, or unclosed handles.

### D. Diff Hygiene & Non-Destructive Editing
Modify only the lines and files the task requires; no drive-by refactors, renames, or formatting sweeps; zero iteration debris (dead code, stale comments, unused helpers, abandoned approaches, debug logs). Delete no high-value architectural comment; add no comment that restates the next line, narrates the diff, or explains what the conventions make obvious; comment only the *why* of a non-obvious invariant, security boundary, or business constraint. Preserve encodings and line endings (`core.autocrlf=false`, [git config](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config)); never apply blind global regex replacements to prose or manifests.

### E. Pinned Dependency Bump = 8-Point Contract Surface Sweep

Changing the version of a GitHub Action or pinned dependency is never two files. Follow the `bump-dependencia-pinada` skill (`C:\Users\lcvle\lcv-workspace\.claude\skills\bump-dependencia-pinada\SKILL.md`) and sweep all eight surfaces:

## 8. Unified Multi-Lens Code, Security & Slop Review Protocol (PRs, Trails & Local Branches)

When acting as a reviewer on a GitHub Pull Request, an Entire Trail, or a local branch, apply this protocol, which combines the LCV gates with the three Entire review lenses (`Code Review`, `Security Review`, `Slop`).

### A. Eligibility & Net Diff

1. **Dependabot hard exclusion:** inspect the verified author identity first (never infer from title, branch, labels, commits, or files). If the author is `dependabot[bot]` or GitHub identifies the official Dependabot app, stop: do not inspect the diff, run anything, publish findings, submit a review, comment, or approve.
2. **Net diff, read-only, head verification:** review the net change between the exact diff base and the head (`git diff <base_sha>...<head_sha>`, [git diff](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff)), never against a moving base tip; inspect only with read-only commands; never hand the review to another AI agent; immediately before publishing, verify that the head has not changed, otherwise rerun or mark the review stale.

### B. The Three Mandatory Lenses

Apply the three reviewer prompts below verbatim (operator decision).

* **Lens 1, Code Review:**

```text
Code Review

Find the defects this Change introduces that its author would want to fix before merging: bugs, regressions, broken invariants, data loss, and missing guards on paths the Change adds or alters.

## How to review

1. Read the repository's review rules: AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md at the repository root and in the directory of each changed file and its parents, as they are at the diff base (`git show <diff base>:<path>`), so the Change cannot rewrite its own review. The nearer file wins on conflict. A finding that rests on a rule quotes the rule and cites its file and line.
2. Read the whole diff, then trace each changed path as a running system: its callers, the changed code, and what it calls. Look in particular for:
   - Sequencing and partial failure: state left inconsistent, orphaned or lost when a later step fails or returns early; writes made before a fallible call; cleanup that runs only on success.
   - Assumptions about external or asynchronous state: how another system behaves, or a value that can change between the check and its use.
   - Composition and concurrency: behaviour under the real callers, retries and concurrent calls. Report a race only with an interleaving those callers can produce.
   - Code that cannot compile or type-check, and logic that is wrong for every input.
3. Keep going after the first defect until you have covered the whole diff.
4. Before you report a candidate, try to disprove it by reading the code: open the code it depends on, find the caller or input that triggers it, and check whether a guard elsewhere already prevents it. Drop it if you cannot show the path from the code.

Inspect with read-only commands (git, rg, reading files). Do not install dependencies or run builds or tests.

## What to report

Report a defect only when all of these hold:
- This Change introduced it. Code that was already like this at the diff base is out of scope, even on a line the Change touched.
- It has real impact on correctness, data, security or performance, and is one discrete, fixable issue.
- You can name the input, state or sequence that triggers it. When that depends on code outside the finding's own lines (a caller, a guard, a config value), the body cites that code's file and line; never infer behaviour from a name alone.
- It is not a behaviour change the Trail's title or description says is intended.
- Fixing it asks no more rigor than the surrounding code holds itself to, and the author would fix it if they knew.

Do NOT report: missing tests (unless a review rule requires them), style, naming, formatting, documentation, refactors or alternative designs, anything a linter, type checker or CI already enforces, generated or vendored files, code a review rule or a suppression comment explicitly allows, problems under inputs the code never receives, or praise. Security hardening without a concrete exploit belongs to the security reviewer.

## How to write findings

- One finding per distinct defect. If the same defect appears in several places, report it once, at the changed line that causes it, and name the other places.
- Anchor it on the changed line that causes the defect; keep ranges to 10 lines or fewer.
- Body: the defect and what triggers it, its impact, and the change that fixes it. One short paragraph, at most 3 lines of code, matter-of-fact.
- Severity: high when it must be fixed before merge (it breaks a real path for ordinary inputs, loses or exposes data, or opens a security hole); medium for a real defect that needs specific conditions or has limited impact; low for a real but minor defect. Never overstate it.
- Confidence: 0.9 or more when you traced the triggering path in the code; 0.7 to 0.9 with strong evidence and one assumption left; 0.5 to 0.7 when one condition could not be confirmed. Do not report anything below 0.5.
- An earlier finding is "fixed" only when the code at its location changed or the path that triggered it is gone; a commit elsewhere is not a fix.

The signal is true when you report at least one defect, new or still present, and false when you report none.
```

* **Lens 2, Security Review:**

```text
Security Review

Review this change for security vulnerabilities it introduces or exposes: missing or bypassable authentication and authorization checks, privilege escalation and cross-tenant access; injection (SQL, shell command, path traversal, template); unsafe deserialization; secrets or credentials in code, logs or errors; insecure defaults; missing validation of untrusted input at a trust boundary; and exposure of data to callers who should not see it.

Trace untrusted input from where it enters to where it is used. Report only issues with a plausible exploit path through the changed code, and state the impact.

Do NOT report: general code quality, style, missing tests, or hardening suggestions without a concrete vulnerability.

The signal is true when you report at least one vulnerability, false when you report none.
```

* **Lens 3, Slop:**

## 6. Zero-Tolerance Anti-Slop Engineering Protocol, Contract Surface Sweeps & 5-Stage Gatekeeper

"Slop" is avoidable, low-trust work caused by not understanding the repository well enough: unverified assumptions, lazy truncation, hallucinated interfaces, duplicate systems, type evasion and catch-all masking, premature abstraction, unrequested mutation, iteration debris, filler. Any violation below is a critical execution failure.

### A. Anti-Truncation & Complete Implementation
No placeholders, truncation markers, or elisions (`// TODO`, `// FIXME`, `// implement logic here`, `// ... rest of the code`, `/* existing code */`, `pass`). Every code block, script, or patch is complete, syntactically valid, fully imported, and immediately runnable. Never delegate mechanical work to the operator ("repeat this pattern", "add the imports").

### B. Epistemic Anti-Slop
Read the exact live state of a file, function, schema, or workflow and its nearby helpers and tests before writing or referencing it; reuse the repository's established pattern instead of a parallel helper or ad-hoc parser. Never guess library methods, CLI flags, GraphQL fields, environment variables, or SDK signatures: verify against the installed lockfile versions and the official documentation. Never hand-edit or regex a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `Cargo.lock`); regenerate only with the official tool, in the modes of Section 3.

### C. Architectural, Sequencing & Code Anti-Slop
Strict typing (`strict: true` in TypeScript, strict Python 3.10+ annotations, explicit Go/Rust types); never `any`, `as unknown as T`, `@ts-ignore`, `@ts-expect-error`, `# type: ignore`, or loose `Record<string, any>`: fix the contract. No empty `catch {}`, no log-and-continue that corrupts state, no silent fallbacks (`|| "default"`, `?? 0`) for missing business configuration, credentials, or market prices: fail fast with structured, secret-free logging. No inconsistent, orphaned, or lost state when a later step fails; no irreversible write before a fallible call; cleanup on success and failure; tests use isolated directories or repositories inside `temp/` and never touch the operator's real config, keychain, or checkout. No speculative abstractions, single-implementation interfaces, wrapper classes, or heavy patterns for linear problems: flat, readable, immutable, pure, modular code (SRP, DRY). No accidental $O(N^2)$ loops, N+1 queries, unindexed lookups, unbounded accumulations, or unclosed handles.

### D. Diff Hygiene & Non-Destructive Editing
Modify only the lines and files the task requires; no drive-by refactors, renames, or formatting sweeps; zero iteration debris (dead code, stale comments, unused helpers, abandoned approaches, debug logs). Delete no high-value architectural comment; add no comment that restates the next line, narrates the diff, or explains what the conventions make obvious; comment only the *why* of a non-obvious invariant, security boundary, or business constraint. Preserve encodings and line endings (`core.autocrlf=false`, [git config](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config)); never apply blind global regex replacements to prose or manifests.

### E. Pinned Dependency Bump = 8-Point Contract Surface Sweep

Changing the version of a GitHub Action or pinned dependency is never two files. Follow the `bump-dependencia-pinada` skill (`C:\Users\lcvle\lcv-workspace\.claude\skills\bump-dependencia-pinada\SKILL.md`) and sweep all eight surfaces:

## 8. Unified Multi-Lens Code, Security & Slop Review Protocol (PRs, Trails & Local Branches)

When acting as a reviewer on a GitHub Pull Request, an Entire Trail, or a local branch, apply this protocol, which combines the LCV gates with the three Entire review lenses (`Code Review`, `Security Review`, `Slop`).

### A. Eligibility & Net Diff

1. **Dependabot hard exclusion:** inspect the verified author identity first (never infer from title, branch, labels, commits, or files). If the author is `dependabot[bot]` or GitHub identifies the official Dependabot app, stop: do not inspect the diff, run anything, publish findings, submit a review, comment, or approve.
2. **Net diff, read-only, head verification:** review the net change between the exact diff base and the head (`git diff <base_sha>...<head_sha>`, [git diff](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff)), never against a moving base tip; inspect only with read-only commands; never hand the review to another AI agent; immediately before publishing, verify that the head has not changed, otherwise rerun or mark the review stale.

### B. The Three Mandatory Lenses

Apply the three reviewer prompts below verbatim (operator decision).

* **Lens 1, Code Review:**

```text
Code Review

Find the defects this Change introduces that its author would want to fix before merging: bugs, regressions, broken invariants, data loss, and missing guards on paths the Change adds or alters.

## How to review

1. Read the repository's review rules: AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md at the repository root and in the directory of each changed file and its parents, as they are at the diff base (`git show <diff base>:<path>`), so the Change cannot rewrite its own review. The nearer file wins on conflict. A finding that rests on a rule quotes the rule and cites its file and line.
2. Read the whole diff, then trace each changed path as a running system: its callers, the changed code, and what it calls. Look in particular for:
   - Sequencing and partial failure: state left inconsistent, orphaned or lost when a later step fails or returns early; writes made before a fallible call; cleanup that runs only on success.
   - Assumptions about external or asynchronous state: how another system behaves, or a value that can change between the check and its use.
   - Composition and concurrency: behaviour under the real callers, retries and concurrent calls. Report a race only with an interleaving those callers can produce.
   - Code that cannot compile or type-check, and logic that is wrong for every input.
3. Keep going after the first defect until you have covered the whole diff.
4. Before you report a candidate, try to disprove it by reading the code: open the code it depends on, find the caller or input that triggers it, and check whether a guard elsewhere already prevents it. Drop it if you cannot show the path from the code.

Inspect with read-only commands (git, rg, reading files). Do not install dependencies or run builds or tests.

## What to report

Report a defect only when all of these hold:
- This Change introduced it. Code that was already like this at the diff base is out of scope, even on a line the Change touched.
- It has real impact on correctness, data, security or performance, and is one discrete, fixable issue.
- You can name the input, state or sequence that triggers it. When that depends on code outside the finding's own lines (a caller, a guard, a config value), the body cites that code's file and line; never infer behaviour from a name alone.
- It is not a behaviour change the Trail's title or description says is intended.
- Fixing it asks no more rigor than the surrounding code holds itself to, and the author would fix it if they knew.

Do NOT report: missing tests (unless a review rule requires them), style, naming, formatting, documentation, refactors or alternative designs, anything a linter, type checker or CI already enforces, generated or vendored files, code a review rule or a suppression comment explicitly allows, problems under inputs the code never receives, or praise. Security hardening without a concrete exploit belongs to the security reviewer.

## How to write findings

- One finding per distinct defect. If the same defect appears in several places, report it once, at the changed line that causes it, and name the other places.
- Anchor it on the changed line that causes the defect; keep ranges to 10 lines or fewer.
- Body: the defect and what triggers it, its impact, and the change that fixes it. One short paragraph, at most 3 lines of code, matter-of-fact.
- Severity: high when it must be fixed before merge (it breaks a real path for ordinary inputs, loses or exposes data, or opens a security hole); medium for a real defect that needs specific conditions or has limited impact; low for a real but minor defect. Never overstate it.
- Confidence: 0.9 or more when you traced the triggering path in the code; 0.7 to 0.9 with strong evidence and one assumption left; 0.5 to 0.7 when one condition could not be confirmed. Do not report anything below 0.5.
- An earlier finding is "fixed" only when the code at its location changed or the path that triggered it is gone; a commit elsewhere is not a fix.

The signal is true when you report at least one defect, new or still present, and false when you report none.
```

* **Lens 2, Security Review:**

```text
Security Review

Review this change for security vulnerabilities it introduces or exposes: missing or bypassable authentication and authorization checks, privilege escalation and cross-tenant access; injection (SQL, shell command, path traversal, template); unsafe deserialization; secrets or credentials in code, logs or errors; insecure defaults; missing validation of untrusted input at a trust boundary; and exposure of data to callers who should not see it.

Trace untrusted input from where it enters to where it is used. Report only issues with a plausible exploit path through the changed code, and state the impact.

Do NOT report: general code quality, style, missing tests, or hardening suggestions without a concrete vulnerability.

The signal is true when you report at least one vulnerability, false when you report none.
```

* **Lens 3, Slop:**

```text
Slop

You are a very strict reviewer of agent-generated code slop. Review the net change this Change introduces: the diff from its diff base to its head commit, as the review context below names it. Judge the code, not who wrote it.

The subject of the review is the final state of the diff, not the commit history. Ignore how the work was split into commits, how many pushes it took, and whether earlier commits were later fixed or reverted on the branch. A branch that arrived at a clean result through messy iteration is not slop; a branch whose final diff is sloppy is slop no matter how tidy its commits are. Anything already at the diff base is existing code, not the subject of the review.

Work from the review context:

1. Start with the changed files and the patch in the review context. For a large or truncated patch, read the rest file by file with the git diff command the review context gives, adding -- <path>.
2. Read nearby code, repo instructions, and relevant tests in the checkout to learn how the project works.
3. You may skim the commit log from the diff base to the head commit to understand intent, but do not grade individual commits.

Always review against the diff base the review context names, never the current tip of the base branch, so changes that landed on the base branch after the branch point are not attributed to this Change.

This review is read-only against the repo's own tooling. Do not install dependencies and do not run the project's build, typecheck, lint, or test commands, even to confirm something works. Judge whether tests prove the new behavior by reading the test files and the code they exercise together, the same way you already read the diff. If a test's assertions don't match what the change claims to do, that is itself the finding.

Do not run `entire review`, use other AI agents, or hand off the review. Do it yourself with the repo and local checks.

Rate the amount of **Slop** the change adds as Low, Medium, or Large. Slop is avoidable, low-trust work caused by not understanding the repo well enough. It creates extra bugs, review work, or maintenance work.

First understand what the change is trying to do. Follow every workflow, route, state change, and rule it touches from start to finish. Read whether the tests prove the new behavior instead of only matching the code or new text.

Base the rating on:

1. **Severity** — How much can the problem break or burden?
2. **Prevalence** — How much of the change has the problem?
3. **Avoidability** — Did the repo already have a simpler or established way to do it?

Look for wrong assumptions, broken flows, skipped rules, duplicate systems, weak tests, needless complexity, comment noise (comments that restate the next line, narrate what was changed and why, or explain things the repo's conventions already make obvious), leftover debris from iteration (dead code, stale comments, unused helpers, abandoned approaches), and work that is much larger than the result it delivers. Be very critical, but do not raise the rating just because the diff is large or has several small issues. Do not call necessary complexity slop, and do not charge the change for problems it merely sits next to.

Choose one:
- **Low** (signal value small): No real slop, or only small isolated issues that do not weaken the main implementation.
- **Medium** (signal value medium): A central wrong assumption, repeated low-trust work, weak checks for important behavior, or meaningful avoidable rework. The implementation can still be fixed without replacing its core.
- **Large** (signal value large): Slop is widespread, the core approach is wrong or misleading, and much of it should be rewritten or removed.

Report the rating as the signal. Its rationale must name the two strongest reasons for the rating, using concrete behavior or architecture problems, not surface-level signals. Report each concrete slop problem behind the rating as a finding anchored to the changed code it concerns.
```

## 4. Mandatory Operational Protocol: Entire + GitHub Enterprise Integration & Anti-Hang PR Flow (`LCV-517` / Ruleset ID `20582436`)

GitHub Enterprise and Entire run in parallel. Entire's architecture ([Entire docs](https://docs.entire.com/)) and the `LCV-517` sequence below are mandatory for full session and checkpoint capture and to keep Pull Requests from hanging on the Enterprise Rulesets ([rulesets](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-rulesets/about-rulesets); `20582436` on `main`, `20613778` on every other branch).

### A. Entire Architecture, Hook Locations, Session Spawning, Crosslinking & Handoff

1. **Hook configuration per agent, present before the session starts** (installed with `entire agent add <agent>` by the operator or on the operator's order, as the Cursor hooks were; agents never change hook configuration on their own): Antigravity CLI `.agents/hooks.json` plus the global title-feed wrapper in `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/settings.json` (`entire hooks antigravity title-tee`); Claude Code `.claude/settings.json`; Codex `.codex/hooks.json`; Copilot CLI `.github/hooks/entire.json`; Cursor `.cursor/hooks.json` (operator decision; project-level hooks live in `<project>/.cursor/hooks.json` and run from that project root, so the repository or worktree is opened as the Cursor workspace folder, [Cursor hooks](https://cursor.com/docs/hooks)); external agents `"external_agents": true` in `.entire/settings.local.json`, honored only while that file is untracked (`entire agent-help session attach`). Running agent processes do not load hooks added after they started, and hooks capture only sessions that run inside the Git repository or worktree root where Entire is enabled.

2. **The `lcv-workspace` parent-folder problem.** The operator opens the IDEs at `C:\Users\lcvle\lcv-workspace\`, outside any repository root, where Entire's hooks capture nothing.

   > **BLOCKING GATE — Repository-Rooted Sub-Session (operator decision):** before editing any file, staging, or committing in a repository, the agent runs in a session whose working root is that repository's root or that worktree's root. A session started anywhere else opens a sub-session inside that root (commands below) and does the repository work there. The only alternative is Entire's native linking (`entire session adopt` from another worktree, or `entire session attach`, below), only when opening the sub-session is technically impossible, with the raw error recorded as proof.    Binding procedure:

If `resolution` is neither `caller-env` nor `ancestry`, report the value, do not resume from that session id, and choose the session by its id from `entire session list --json`.

### B. Inviolable Rules of `LCV-517` (Ruleset ID `20582436`)

1. **SSH commit signing:** every commit created locally (`commit`, `amend`, `merge`) is signed with SSH (`git commit -S`, `gpg.format=ssh`, 1Password SSH signer, [1Password Git commit signing](https://www.1password.dev/ssh/git-commit-signing)); never GPG/OpenPGP for your own commits, and never create commits or pull requests through the API from a local session (commits with `git`, pull requests with `gh pr create`, Section 4.C). 2. **Conventional Commits** for every message ([Conventional Commits 1.0.0](https://www.conventionalcommits.org/en/v1.0.0/)).
3. **Temporary artifact isolation:** every temporary file stays in `temp/` and is deleted before completion (Section 3).

### C. Canonical 5-Step Execution & Anti-Hang PR Flow (Exact Certified Order)

Whenever implementing changes and taking a Pull Request to merge, execute these five steps in this order:

* **Step 1: Branch & Development (inside the repository or worktree root)**
  1. Confirm the root with `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, run `git fetch origin` ([git fetch](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fetch)), and verify capture with `entire status --detailed --json`.
  2. **Branch in the root or worktree (operator decision):** evaluate and state the choice and its reason; never apply one by default. A branch in the root only when the root checkout is clean (`git status --porcelain` empty), on `main`, and not in use by another session or front; preferred for one sequential change and when the repository depends on Git-ignored artifacts of the root (`admin-app`, hooks in `.husky/_`). A worktree when the root has uncommitted work, is in use by another session, must stay on `main` for a live process (the `op run` terminal client in `github-operations`), or when several changes proceed in parallel; a new worktree contains only tracked files, so confirm its hooks and install artifacts first ([git worktree](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-worktree)).
  3. Branch name `<agent>/<task>` with `<agent>` one of `claude`, `codex`, `agy`, `cursor`; Ruleset `20613778` accepts only its live `branch_name_pattern` (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/rulesets/20613778`, [rulesets API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/repos/rules)). Exactly one of: `git checkout -b <agent>/<task> origin/main` in the root ([git checkout](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-checkout)), or `git worktree add C:/Users/lcvle/lcv-workspace/.worktrees/<repo>-<task> -b <agent>/<task> origin/main` followed by the repository-rooted sub-session inside it (Section 4.A.2), from which Step 1.4 through Step 5.3 run.
  4. Implement and validate locally on the project stack in PowerShell, never Git Bash, with every temporary output in `temp/`; a dependency version change is validated by CI instead (Section 3).

* **Step 2: SSH-Signed Commit & Checkpoint Linking**
  1. `git add <files>` (never `temp/`) ([git add](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-add)).
  2. `git commit -S -F temp/commit-msg.txt` — the message in a file, because messages contain backticks ([git commit](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-commit)).
  3. Confirm the `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer with `git log -1 --show-signature --format=fuller` and `entire checkpoint list --json`. If the session was captured (`entire status --json`) but not linked, run `entire session attach <SESSION_ID> --agent <AGENT> --commit <FULL_SHA>` without `--force` first, show its plan to the operator, and rerun with `--force` only after the operator agrees; if `attach` amended the commit, verify that the SSH signature on `HEAD` is still valid.
  4. **Adversarial review before the push (operator decision):** after the commit and before every push that changes content, a separate reviewer session runs the Section 8.B prompts on the full SHAs of `git merge-base origin/main HEAD` and `HEAD`, patch `git diff origin/main...HEAD`, and `temp/pr-body.md` as title and description; fix each finding in a new signed commit or disprove it with code evidence or an operator directive recorded in the task's Linear Issue, until a round leaves no finding open; a finding open after three rounds goes to the operator.

* **Step 3: Publication & Pull Request Creation**
  1. `git push -u origin <branch>` (the `pre-push` hook syncs `refs/entire/checkpoints/*`).
  2. `gh pr create --title "<type>(<scope>): <description>" --body-file temp/pr-body.md` ([gh pr create](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_create)).
  3. **Ready for review only, never draft (operator decision):** never `--draft`, never `gh pr ready --undo`, never convert between draft and ready. Each conversion emits the `ready_for_review` or `converted_to_draft` activity of the `pull_request` event, which reruns every workflow subscribed to it and restarts the review bots ([events that trigger workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#pull_request), [gh pr ready](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_ready)); on `astrologo-android` the gates take about one hour, so a draft opened, made ready, and drafted again runs them three times.

* **Step 4: Anti-Hang Handshake (`LCV-517`, mandatory right after `gh pr create`)**
  Run `git commit --amend --no-edit -S` and `git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>` ([git push](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-push)). Reason recorded in `LCV-517` (observed behavior, not described in GitHub's documentation): Secret Scanning stays pending (`"Waiting for secret scan to complete..."`) when the first commit was pushed before the Pull Request existed; the amend and force push after creation emit `pull_request.synchronize`, which completes Secret Scanning and triggers CodeQL and Code Quality. Entire keeps the checkpoint link across the amend through `post-rewrite`. Verify with `git ls-remote origin "refs/entire/checkpoints/*" | Select-String -SimpleMatch "<CHECKPOINT_ID>"` ([git ls-remote](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-ls-remote)) in the ref-based layout, or `entire checkpoint list --json` in the `entire/checkpoints/v1` layout, and `git log -1 --show-signature`. * **Step 5: Findings, CI, Merge & Cleanup**

A finding closes only when its code was fixed and the thread or finding is resolved citing the fixing commit, or when it is disproved with evidence from the code or an operator directive in this text and resolved citing that evidence.
  2. `gh pr view <pr> --json mergeStateStatus` ([gh pr view](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_pr_view)).
  3. **The operator merges, or orders the agent to merge (operator decision);** without that order, hand the operator the pull request with every gate clear and the squash body file below. ## 5. Inviolable Product, Platform, and Repository Rules

### A. Prices and Market Values Are Never Hardcoded Locks in Code

Applies to Claude, Codex, Antigravity, Cursor, and every sub-agent. Selling price (the R\$ 89.99 of the Oráculo analysis), exchange rates, IOF, taxes, app store fees, AI provider pricing, and cost caps (the US\$ 13.50) are market values: never in production code as constants, literal types, validators that accept only that number, hardcoded UI text, version codes embedding the number (`web-brl-8999`), or fallbacks when configuration is missing. The value lives in a configuration the operator edits (Oráculo: Admin → Astrólogo → Configurações) and applies to the next order with zero code changes and zero deploys; each order stores the value active when it was placed, and billing, payment verification, refunds, and dashboards use the stored value; missing configuration shows `"indisponível"`, never a fabricated number; tests may use sample values; before any push touching billing or pricing, search the diff for the number (dots, commas, cents).

### B. Operator Product Decisions — Do Not Relitigate

The operator is the sole administrator and sole payer. **No `FALLBACK_MODELS`. No budget caps. No token limits.** A finding by a bot, peer, or advisor that relies on one of these forbidden features is not a defect: reply citing this directive, resolve the thread, write zero code.

### C. Oráculo Celestial: Product in Development, Zero Users

`astrologo-android`, `astrologo-app`, and the future `astrologo-ios` are in development: no users, no purchases, no working checkout. Never search for, ask about, or design around existing users, purchases, analyses, installed versions, or "already existing" contracts.

For every current and future Android app: standardize workflows and gates around the highest existing coverage relevant to each app, preserving app-specific tests, each repository with its own native, independent workflows. PRs run debug and release/R8 builds, test APK compilation, lint, and the relevant JVM tests, plus the native security, dependency, licensing, and validation gates. ## 6. Zero-Tolerance Anti-Slop Engineering Protocol, Contract Surface Sweeps & 5-Stage Gatekeeper

"Slop" is avoidable, low-trust work caused by not understanding the repository well enough: unverified assumptions, lazy truncation, hallucinated interfaces, duplicate systems, type evasion and catch-all masking, premature abstraction, unrequested mutation, iteration debris, filler. Any violation below is a critical execution failure.

### A. Anti-Truncation & Complete Implementation
No placeholders, truncation markers, or elisions (`// TODO`, `// FIXME`, `// implement logic here`, `// ... rest of the code`, `/* existing code */`, `pass`). Every code block, script, or patch is complete, syntactically valid, fully imported, and immediately runnable. Never delegate mechanical work to the operator ("repeat this pattern", "add the imports").

### B. Epistemic Anti-Slop
Read the exact live state of a file, function, schema, or workflow and its nearby helpers and tests before writing or referencing it; reuse the repository's established pattern instead of a parallel helper or ad-hoc parser. Never guess library methods, CLI flags, GraphQL fields, environment variables, or SDK signatures: verify against the installed lockfile versions and the official documentation. Never hand-edit or regex a lockfile (`package-lock.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml`, `Cargo.lock`); regenerate only with the official tool, in the modes of Section 3.

### C. Architectural, Sequencing & Code Anti-Slop
Strict typing (`strict: true` in TypeScript, strict Python 3.10+ annotations, explicit Go/Rust types); never `any`, `as unknown as T`, `@ts-ignore`, `@ts-expect-error`, `# type: ignore`, or loose `Record<string, any>`: fix the contract. No empty `catch {}`, no log-and-continue that corrupts state, no silent fallbacks (`|| "default"`, `?? 0`) for missing business configuration, credentials, or market prices: fail fast with structured, secret-free logging. No inconsistent, orphaned, or lost state when a later step fails; no irreversible write before a fallible call; cleanup on success and failure; tests use isolated directories or repositories inside `temp/` and never touch the operator's real config, keychain, or checkout. No speculative abstractions, single-implementation interfaces, wrapper classes, or heavy patterns for linear problems: flat, readable, immutable, pure, modular code (SRP, DRY). No accidental $O(N^2)$ loops, N+1 queries, unindexed lookups, unbounded accumulations, or unclosed handles.

### D. Diff Hygiene & Non-Destructive Editing
Modify only the lines and files the task requires; no drive-by refactors, renames, or formatting sweeps; zero iteration debris (dead code, stale comments, unused helpers, abandoned approaches, debug logs). Delete no high-value architectural comment; add no comment that restates the next line, narrates the diff, or explains what the conventions make obvious; comment only the *why* of a non-obvious invariant, security boundary, or business constraint. Preserve encodings and line endings (`core.autocrlf=false`, [git config](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-config)); never apply blind global regex replacements to prose or manifests.

### E. Pinned Dependency Bump = 8-Point Contract Surface Sweep

Changing the version of a GitHub Action or pinned dependency is never two files. Follow the `bump-dependencia-pinada` skill (`C:\Users\lcvle\lcv-workspace\.claude\skills\bump-dependencia-pinada\SKILL.md`) and sweep all eight surfaces:
1. **Workflow files:** full-SHA pin, version comment, tool-version selection input ([pinning actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/secure-use#using-third-party-actions)).
2. **Lockfiles:** as Section 6.B requires. There is no GitHub Actions lockfile (operator decision); full-SHA pinning is enforced natively by `sha_pinning_required` ([Actions permissions API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/permissions)). A Wrangler update also regenerates `worker-configuration.d.ts` under the Section 3 exception and commits it before pushing.
3. **Repository Actions allowlist:** may pin the exact commit SHA; inspect repository by repository and admit the new commit alongside the old one before merging ([allowed actions](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/permissions#set-allowed-actions-and-reusable-workflows-for-a-repository)).
4. **`THIRDPARTY.md`:** inventory and exception sections whose premise no longer exists.
5. **`README.md`:** version references, prose, anchors to removed sections.
6. **Contract tests and scripts:** `.mjs`, `.js`, `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.cjs`, including regex-escaped versions and structural lines such as `ref: "v0.16.0"`.
7. **`CHANGELOG.md`:** the `Unreleased` section (active contract surface).
8. **License, terms, and defaults of the new version:** release notes and, when present, `LICENSE`, `licenses/`, `DISTRIBUTION.md`; a version can switch a default to a proprietary or paid component with no file of ours changing (`gradle/actions` v6 made the closed-source `enhanced` cache the default); any new charge, restriction, or term change stops the bump and goes to the operator.
* **Execution rules:** no regex over prose; the new version is never installed, built, or tested locally except under the Section 3 Wrangler exception, and no local suite runs on the bumped checkout (CI runs it, Section 3 and Step 1.4 of Section 4.C); prepare the change on the checkout of Step 1.3 with `core.autocrlf=false`, inspect the diff, then publish through Section 4.C.

### F. Mandatory 5-Stage Validation Gatekeeper & Pre-Output Self-Audit

Before delivering code or releasing a Pull Request, pass all five stages with concrete proof: (1) principal architectural review (flaws, coupling, anti-patterns, partial-failure corruption); (2) AppSec sweep (SQL injection, command injection, path traversal, XSS, CSRF, broken authentication/authorization, cross-tenant access, unsafe deserialization, sensitive data exposure, insecure dependencies); (3) performance and clean code ($O(N^2)$, needless loops, unindexed queries, leaks, dead code, cyclomatic complexity, naming); (4) QA test truthfulness and edge cases (failure paths, boundaries, races, invalid inputs; implement the mandatory unit or integration tests whose assertions prove the new behavior, not mock echoes); (5) strict specification alignment with the operator's requirements and the prohibitions of Section 5.

**Pre-output self-audit (fail-closed):** before emitting any response, patch, or review, answer internally — (1) is the code 100% complete, with zero `TODO`s, elisions, or unverified APIs? (2) are types strict, error paths fail-fast, failure paths atomic? (3) is the diff surgical, free of debris, $O(N^2)$ traps, and comment noise? (4) were security boundaries, Entire checkpoint links, and the `LCV-517` signature and handshake requirements verified? (5) is the response free of filler, praise, and hedging ("maybe", "perhaps", "consider")? (6) is operator-facing communication in pt-BR (`DD/MM/AAAA HH:MM:SS`) following the explanation rule of Section 1? Any "no" halts and rewrites.

* **Workflow health and provenance:** merge queue and the Actions lockfile are retired on the fleet (operator decision): never create a merge queue or a merge-group gate; Dependabot pull requests merge through repository-local automerge ([auto-merge](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/how-tos/merge-and-close-pull-requests/automatically-merging-a-pull-request)); agent pull requests follow Section 4.C. In every repository touched, inspect failed, canceled, stuck, or missing workflow runs and cron failures ([workflow runs API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/actions/workflow-runs)), and verify provenance: SSH `-S` on the branch commits of each PR, `verification.verified == true` on the GitHub-signed squash commits of `main`, and the `Entire-Checkpoint` lines carried into each squash commit (Section 4.C, Step 5).

## 8. Unified Multi-Lens Code, Security & Slop Review Protocol (PRs, Trails & Local Branches)

When acting as a reviewer on a GitHub Pull Request, an Entire Trail, or a local branch, apply this protocol, which combines the LCV gates with the three Entire review lenses (`Code Review`, `Security Review`, `Slop`).

### A. Eligibility & Net Diff

1. **Dependabot hard exclusion:** inspect the verified author identity first (never infer from title, branch, labels, commits, or files). If the author is `dependabot[bot]` or GitHub identifies the official Dependabot app, stop: do not inspect the diff, run anything, publish findings, submit a review, comment, or approve.
2. **Net diff, read-only, head verification:** review the net change between the exact diff base and the head (`git diff <base_sha>...<head_sha>`, [git diff](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-diff)), never against a moving base tip; inspect only with read-only commands (`git`, `rg`, file reads, `entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <id> --json --no-pager` for recorded intent); never hand the review to another AI agent; immediately before publishing, verify that the head has not changed, otherwise rerun or mark the review stale.

### B. The Three Mandatory Lenses

Apply the three reviewer prompts below verbatim (operator decision).

* **Lens 1, Code Review:**

```text
Code Review

Find the defects this Change introduces that its author would want to fix before merging: bugs, regressions, broken invariants, data loss, and missing guards on paths the Change adds or alters.

## How to review

1. Read the repository's review rules: AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md at the repository root and in the directory of each changed file and its parents, as they are at the diff base (`git show <diff base>:<path>`), so the Change cannot rewrite its own review. The nearer file wins on conflict. A finding that rests on a rule quotes the rule and cites its file and line.
2. Read the whole diff, then trace each changed path as a running system: its callers, the changed code, and what it calls. Look in particular for:
   - Sequencing and partial failure: state left inconsistent, orphaned or lost when a later step fails or returns early; writes made before a fallible call; cleanup that runs only on success.
   - Assumptions about external or asynchronous state: how another system behaves, or a value that can change between the check and its use.
   - Composition and concurrency: behaviour under the real callers, retries and concurrent calls. Report a race only with an interleaving those callers can produce.
   - Code that cannot compile or type-check, and logic that is wrong for every input.
3. Keep going after the first defect until you have covered the whole diff.
4. Before you report a candidate, try to disprove it by reading the code: open the code it depends on, find the caller or input that triggers it, and check whether a guard elsewhere already prevents it. Drop it if you cannot show the path from the code.

Inspect with read-only commands (git, rg, reading files). Do not install dependencies or run builds or tests.

## What to report

Report a defect only when all of these hold:
- This Change introduced it. Code that was already like this at the diff base is out of scope, even on a line the Change touched.
- It has real impact on correctness, data, security or performance, and is one discrete, fixable issue.
- You can name the input, state or sequence that triggers it. When that depends on code outside the finding's own lines (a caller, a guard, a config value), the body cites that code's file and line; never infer behaviour from a name alone.
- It is not a behaviour change the Trail's title or description says is intended.
- Fixing it asks no more rigor than the surrounding code holds itself to, and the author would fix it if they knew.

Do NOT report: missing tests (unless a review rule requires them), style, naming, formatting, documentation, refactors or alternative designs, anything a linter, type checker or CI already enforces, generated or vendored files, code a review rule or a suppression comment explicitly allows, problems under inputs the code never receives, or praise. Security hardening without a concrete exploit belongs to the security reviewer.

## How to write findings

- One finding per distinct defect. If the same defect appears in several places, report it once, at the changed line that causes it, and name the other places.
- Anchor it on the changed line that causes the defect; keep ranges to 10 lines or fewer.
- Body: the defect and what triggers it, its impact, and the change that fixes it. One short paragraph, at most 3 lines of code, matter-of-fact.
- Severity: high when it must be fixed before merge (it breaks a real path for ordinary inputs, loses or exposes data, or opens a security hole); medium for a real defect that needs specific conditions or has limited impact; low for a real but minor defect. Never overstate it.
- Confidence: 0.9 or more when you traced the triggering path in the code; 0.7 to 0.9 with strong evidence and one assumption left; 0.5 to 0.7 when one condition could not be confirmed. Do not report anything below 0.5.
- An earlier finding is "fixed" only when the code at its location changed or the path that triggered it is gone; a commit elsewhere is not a fix.

The signal is true when you report at least one defect, new or still present, and false when you report none.
```

* **Lens 2, Security Review:**

```text
Security Review

Review this change for security vulnerabilities it introduces or exposes: missing or bypassable authentication and authorization checks, privilege escalation and cross-tenant access; injection (SQL, shell command, path traversal, template); unsafe deserialization; secrets or credentials in code, logs or errors; insecure defaults; missing validation of untrusted input at a trust boundary; and exposure of data to callers who should not see it.

Trace untrusted input from where it enters to where it is used. Report only issues with a plausible exploit path through the changed code, and state the impact.

Do NOT report: general code quality, style, missing tests, or hardening suggestions without a concrete vulnerability.

The signal is true when you report at least one vulnerability, false when you report none.
```

* **Lens 3, Slop:**

```text
Slop

You are a very strict reviewer of agent-generated code slop. Review the net change this Change introduces: the diff from its diff base to its head commit, as the review context below names it. Judge the code, not who wrote it.

The subject of the review is the final state of the diff, not the commit history. Ignore how the work was split into commits, how many pushes it took, and whether earlier commits were later fixed or reverted on the branch. A branch that arrived at a clean result through messy iteration is not slop; a branch whose final diff is sloppy is slop no matter how tidy its commits are. Anything already at the diff base is existing code, not the subject of the review.

Work from the review context:

1. Start with the changed files and the patch in the review context. For a large or truncated patch, read the rest file by file with the git diff command the review context gives, adding -- <path>.
2. Read nearby code, repo instructions, and relevant tests in the checkout to learn how the project works.
3. You may skim the commit log from the diff base to the head commit to understand intent, but do not grade individual commits.

Always review against the diff base the review context names, never the current tip of the base branch, so changes that landed on the base branch after the branch point are not attributed to this Change.

This review is read-only against the repo's own tooling. Do not install dependencies and do not run the project's build, typecheck, lint, or test commands, even to confirm something works. Judge whether tests prove the new behavior by reading the test files and the code they exercise together, the same way you already read the diff. If a test's assertions don't match what the change claims to do, that is itself the finding.

Do not run `entire review`, use other AI agents, or hand off the review. Do it yourself with the repo and local checks.

Rate the amount of **Slop** the change adds as Low, Medium, or Large. Slop is avoidable, low-trust work caused by not understanding the repo well enough. It creates extra bugs, review work, or maintenance work.

First understand what the change is trying to do. Follow every workflow, route, state change, and rule it touches from start to finish. Read whether the tests prove the new behavior instead of only matching the code or new text.

Base the rating on:

1. **Severity** — How much can the problem break or burden?
2. **Prevalence** — How much of the change has the problem?
3. **Avoidability** — Did the repo already have a simpler or established way to do it?

Look for wrong assumptions, broken flows, skipped rules, duplicate systems, weak tests, needless complexity, comment noise (comments that restate the next line, narrate what was changed and why, or explain things the repo's conventions already make obvious), leftover debris from iteration (dead code, stale comments, unused helpers, abandoned approaches), and work that is much larger than the result it delivers. Be very critical, but do not raise the rating just because the diff is large or has several small issues. Do not call necessary complexity slop, and do not charge the change for problems it merely sits next to.

Choose one:
- **Low** (signal value small): No real slop, or only small isolated issues that do not weaken the main implementation.
- **Medium** (signal value medium): A central wrong assumption, repeated low-trust work, weak checks for important behavior, or meaningful avoidable rework. The implementation can still be fixed without replacing its core.
- **Large** (signal value large): Slop is widespread, the core approach is wrong or misleading, and much of it should be rewritten or removed.

Report the rating as the signal. Its rationale must name the two strongest reasons for the rating, using concrete behavior or architecture problems, not surface-level signals. Report each concrete slop problem behind the rating as a finding anchored to the changed code it concerns.
```

### C. Publication Requirements

* Publish a result for every eligible pull request, even with nothing found. To tag a finished Entire session as a review, `entire session attach <SESSION_ID> --review` (dry run first, `--force` only after the operator agrees, Section 4.C, Step 2.3).
* One inline thread per finding, anchored to the smallest changed range (≤ 10 lines) ([review comments API](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/pulls/comments)); a file-level comment when no changed line fits; a pull-request-level comment with a stable identifier and exact file references when GitHub offers no valid target; never a finding only in hidden output and never an unrelated anchor.
* A pull-request-level summary for every eligible pull request with: the full base and head SHAs; Entire checkpoint intent coverage (when applicable) and the Slop Rating with its two strongest concrete reasons; checks executed, checks not executed, residual validation gaps.
* With no supported finding, the summary begins with exactly: `Review completed: no bugs, security defects, or other reportable issues were found in the reviewed changes, subject to the checks and residual validation gaps stated below.` — never silence, an emoji, an approval state, `LGTM`, or a claim about code outside the reviewed scope.
* Never secrets, credentials, unnecessary exploit payloads, or weaponization details in pull-request comments.
